newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Placer Dome positive on Asia despite Bre-X.
newsitem.headline: Placer Dome positive on Asia despite Bre-X.

text.p: Canadian mining giant Placer Dome continues to look for opportunities in Asia, although the recent Bre-X scandal in Indonesia has made investors more cautious, the firm's chief said on Thursday.

"It's clear our future will be closely bound with the Asia Pacific rim region," John Willson, president and chief executive officer of Placer Dome Inc told the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong.
He said while Latin America and North America had received large amounts of the world's exploration dollars, Asia had seen the fastest expansion in investment.
About $400 million in exploration was spent in Asia in 1996, a 61 percent increase over 1995, Willson said.
Although more regulation was needed, it was difficult to prevent another Bre-X-type situtation taking place, he added.

"It's a testimony to how cleverly the thing (the scam) had been done. It had momentum, it managed to survive for a long time. Iit's incredible that people could do the sorting of the samples for so long and so cleverly it didn't leak," he said.

A report by consultant Strathcona Mineral Services released earlier this month found evidence of tampering with core samples taken from Canadian junior miner Bre-X's gold exploration site at Busang, in East Kalimantan, Indonesia, previously billed as the gold find of the century.
Bre-X held a 45 percent stake in the project, Freeport McMoRan Copper and Gold of the U.S. 15 percent and the Indonesian government and other Indonesian interests the rest.
But Busang has taken its toll on Canadian mining, with not as much capital available for mining operations, Willson said.

"There's a feeling in North America that anyone in Bre-X was a fool, and as it turns out, they were. People do put up money without digging their own holes," he said, adding that few people understood the importance of due diligence confirmation. "It will take a while to go away. We have to make ourselves better understood. We have done a bad job in the past."
Asked if he saw the squeeze on funds available to the small exploration companies caused by the Busang scam creating opportunities for acquisitions of these junior miners, Willson said:

"Yes we do. The juniors in Canada have been multipyling, they have been stealing excellent people, from Placer Dome among others, raising money in the capital market. That has meant that the pool of projects has dried up."
He said the junior mining companies were increasingly looking to the larger mining firms for backing.

In China, Placer's enthusiasm for investment has been dampened by the lack of a clear legal framework, confusion over lines of central and provincial government authority, a vague Mineral Resource Law, and the Chinese central bank's total control over gold sales. Willson said.
Placer sees gold being at an average of $375 per ounce over the next 10 years, he said.
China's domestic gold prices, usually below international levels, is another factor which has made investment in the country difficult, Willson said.
In comparison, the Venezuelan central bank has shown flexibility in its policy towards Placer's project there.
Placer holds a 70 percent interest in Venezuela's Las Cristinas gold property.
The Venezuelan central bank has agreed Placer need only to sell 20 percent of its gold production to the bank and may market the rest at international prices, he said.
Placer Dome was still waiting clarification on a few key issues connected with its Venezuelan project, but hopes it will go ahead shortly, Willson said, without providing details.

Crystallex International Corp announced in March it had acquired the rights to Las Cristinas, a contention vigorously disputed by Placer, Venezuelan officials, and CVG, the Venezuelan state-owned company which is Placer's partner in the project.
